title: Bering and the Great Northern Expedition
intro: The Great Northern Expedition, conceived by Peter the Great and led by Vitus Bering, was a Russian expedition of roughly 1733 to 1743 that mapped most of the Arctic coast of Siberia and much of the Arctic coast of North America. Bering led one of its two Pacific divisions, with the aim of finding the sea route to North America.
ending: Bering died of scurvy on 8 December 1741 on what later became known as Bering Island. The 46 survivors built a boat from the wreckage and sailed for Petropavlovsk in August 1742, carrying sea otter pelts that sparked Russian settlement in Alaska.

stops.text: The two Pacific divisions of the expedition, led by Martin Spanberg and Vitus Bering, left the capital in February and April 1733. The academic group followed on 8 August 1733.
stops.quote: The two Pacific divisions of the expedition, led by Martin Spanberg and Vitus Bering, left St. Petersburg in February and April 1733, while the academic group departed on August 8, 1733.

stops.text: The academic party reached Yakutsk, where almost all members of the two Pacific divisions had already gathered, so that the scholars had trouble finding lodgings. The scholars were to travel on to Kamchatka with Bering.
stops.quote: They reached Yakutsk in September 1736. Almost all the members of the two Pacific divisions of the expedition had gathered there in the meantime, and as a result, Gmelin and Müller experienced difficulties in locating accommodation.

stops.text: The St. Peter and the St. Paul set sail from Petropavlovsk. Six days later fog separated them, and both ships kept sailing east.
stops.quote: In June 1741, the ships St. Peter and the St. Paul set sail from Petropavlovsk. Six days later they lost sight of each other in a thick fog, but both vessels continued to sail east.

stops.text: Bering and the crew of the St. Peter sighted a towering peak on the Alaska mainland. Bering was anxious to return to Russia and turned westward.
stops.quote: On roughly July 16, 1741, Bering and the crew of St. Peter sighted a towering peak on the Alaska mainland, Mount Saint Elias.

stops.text: Bering anchored off the island while crew members went ashore to explore and find water. The naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller walked around the island and recorded its plants and wildlife.
stops.quote: He later anchored his vessel off Kayak Island while crew members went ashore to explore and find water.

stops.text: Storms battered the ship, which was wrecked on the shore of the island that many of the crew took for the coast of Kamchatka. Bering fell sick with scurvy and died there on 8 December 1741. Of those left, 28 died over the winter.
stops.quote: Bering's ship was battered by storms, and in November his ship was wrecked on the shore of Bering Island, which many of the crew thought to be the coast of Kamchatka.

stops.text: When the weather improved, the 46 survivors built a 40-foot boat from the wreckage and sailed for Petropavlovsk. Bering's crew reached the shore of Kamchatka in 1742 with word of the expedition.
stops.quote: When weather improved, the 46 survivors built a 40-foot (12 m) boat from the wreckage and set sail for Petropavlovsk in August 1742.

notes: The article gives Bering's own route thinly: nothing on the crossing of Siberia beyond Yakutsk, and Okhotsk is not mentioned at all, so no Okhotsk stop. The Yakutsk date (September 1736) is when Gmelin and Müller arrived; the article gives no arrival date for Bering himself, and does not say how he reached Petropavlovsk. Chirikov's landfall (probably Prince of Wales Island, 15 July 1741) and his two lost landing parties belong to the other ship and are left out; the academic group's route (Tobolsk, Irkutsk, Lena) is left out too. Kayak Island has no date in the article. The article says the Aleut were first recorded by Steller but names no place for it, so no Aleutian stop. The final stop's sailing date is August 1742; the article says only that the crew reached Kamchatka in 1742. The article says the Pacific party left in 'February and April 1733' without saying which division left when. Article is sceptical-free but its 'European discovery of Alaska' wording was not used.
